title: How Much Electricity Does an HVAC System Use?
h1: How Much Electricity Does a Home HVAC System Use?
description: HVAC electricity use depends on system type, size, efficiency, run time and your home. Here's what uses the most power and how to estimate your own use.
quick_answer: It depends on the type of system, its size and efficiency, and how many hours it runs. Central air conditioners and heat pumps use the most electricity, mainly through the compressor and outdoor fan. A gas furnace uses electricity only for its blower and controls. Cooling is usually the biggest HVAC electric load in San Diego and Orange County homes, especially inland.
body:
Which parts of an HVAC system use electricity?

  • Compressor: the biggest user. It runs whenever an AC or heat pump is actively cooling or heating.
  • Outdoor fan: runs with the compressor to move heat out of or into the outdoor coil.
  • Indoor blower: moves air through the ducts. It runs any time the system heats, cools or the fan is set to on.
  • Backup heat strips: on many heat pumps. These use a lot of power when they run, so they're meant for defrost and backup only.
  • Controls and thermostat: small, steady draw.

A gas furnace burns gas for heat, so its electric use is mostly the blower. An electric furnace or heat strips turn electricity straight into heat, which uses much more power than a heat pump doing the same job.

How can I estimate how much mine uses?

You can get a rough idea with information from the unit and your bill:

  1. Find the electrical ratings. The label on the outdoor unit lists its electrical data. A technician can tell you the actual running draw, which is usually less than the maximum listed.
  2. Estimate run time. A smart thermostat often reports how many hours the system ran each day or month.
  3. Multiply. Running power in kilowatts times hours of operation gives kilowatt-hours, the unit your utility bills you in.
  4. Compare seasons. Look at your bill for a mild spring month and a hot summer month. The difference is a rough picture of what cooling adds.

Many San Diego and Orange County utility customers are on time-of-use rate plans, where electricity costs more in the late afternoon and evening. When your AC runs matters as well as how long.

What makes an HVAC system use more electricity?

  • Low efficiency: older systems with lower SEER2 (cooling) or HSPF2 (heat pump heating) ratings use more power for the same cooling or heating.
  • Wrong size: an oversized system short cycles, and an undersized one runs constantly on hot days.
  • Dirty filter or coils: restricted airflow and dirty coils make the compressor work harder.
  • Leaky attic ducts: cooled or heated air escapes into a hot or cold attic before it reaches your rooms.
  • Thin attic insulation: common in older homes, it lets summer heat pour in through the ceiling.
  • Low refrigerant: the system runs longer to deliver less cooling.
  • Thermostat habits: large setpoint swings and running the fan on all day add up.

How can you lower HVAC electricity use?

  • Change the filter on schedule and keep the outdoor unit clear.
  • Set the thermostat a few degrees higher in summer, and use a schedule instead of manual changes.
  • Pre-cool the house earlier in the day if you're on a time-of-use plan, then let it coast through the peak hours.
  • Set the fan to auto instead of on.
  • Close blinds on west- and south-facing windows on hot afternoons.
  • Have attic ducts sealed and insulation checked.
  • Get a yearly tune-up so a technician can clean coils and check refrigerant and electrical parts.

Does a heat pump use a lot of electricity in winter?

Less than many people expect. A heat pump moves heat from outdoor air instead of making it, so it delivers more heat than it uses in electricity. In our mild winters, it usually runs efficiently. The thing to watch is backup heat strips. If they come on often during mild weather, something may be set wrong or need repair.

When is a new system worth it for energy savings?

If your system is older, needs frequent repairs or can't keep up on hot days, a properly sized, higher-efficiency system can use noticeably less electricity. Variable-speed heat pumps and air conditioners tend to run longer at low speed, which keeps temperatures steadier and avoids the energy spikes of frequent starts.

What should I do if my bills seem too high?

Start with the filter and thermostat settings. If those look fine, have the system checked for refrigerant, airflow and duct leaks. Our HVAC team can find out where the energy is going and recommend repairs or upgrades, with a free estimate on any replacement.
faqs: Does running the fan all day use a lot of electricity?
It uses more than leaving it on auto, especially with an older single-speed blower motor. Newer variable-speed blowers use much less at low speed.
Does a gas furnace use electricity?
Yes, but not much compared with an AC. The blower motor, igniter, inducer fan and controls all run on electricity, while the heat itself comes from gas.
Is it cheaper to leave the AC on all day?
Usually not. Raising the setpoint while you're away and letting it cool before you return tends to use less energy. On time-of-use plans, pre-cooling before the peak can help.
Do heat pumps use more electricity than air conditioners?
In cooling mode they use about the same. In winter a heat pump uses electricity to heat too, but it's far more efficient than electric resistance heat.
